title: The Freezer Multisig's 2-of-5 threshold lets Operational GovOps trigger a freeze alone, since it controls three of the five seats
content:
A.6.1.1.7.2.6.1.2.1.2.1.3.3 lists the Freezer Multisig's signers as "three (3) addresses controlled by Operational GovOps Soter Labs, one (1) address controlled by Operational Facilitator Redline Facilitation Group, and one (1) address controlled by Osero." A.6.1.1.7.2.6.1.2.1.2.1.3.2 sets the threshold at 2 of 5.

The composition looks tri-party, and the mandate reads as a shared safety function: signers "should exercise their authority to remove a compromised or malicious Actor ... in the event of an emergency," with each action "reported to the Sky community within a reasonable time frame."

But the arithmetic does not match the appearance. Two of Soter Labs' three seats satisfy the threshold on their own, so Operational GovOps can revoke an Actor without the Facilitator or Osero agreeing. Conversely, Osero and the Facilitator together also reach 2 — so no party is excluded, but only one party can act entirely alone.

The low threshold is defensible on its own terms. A freeze is a defensive, narrow action: it removes an Actor's ability to submit operations and, per A.6.1.1.7.2.6.1.2.2.3.1, leaves the Allocator Role untouched. Making it hard to trigger would be the greater risk during a live key compromise, and the damage from a wrongful freeze is bounded and reversible.

Still, the effective unilateralism is worth recording. The party that can freeze Osero's operator is also the party that supplies the alternative operator (the Core Operator Relayer Multisig) and the party that verifies Osero's rebate calculation — three concentrations of the same counterparty, with only ex-post reporting as the check.
description: Signers are 3 Soter Labs, 1 Redline Facilitation Group, 1 Osero; the low threshold makes emergency revocation easy but leaves it exercisable by one party unilaterally.
